result:
Solution 3 is the most likely to be correct, though I did not fully verify its derivation.

**Solution 1** gives 1/n, which does not depend on k. The problem asks for a threshold as a function of k, so this is unlikely. Its claim that a candidate with the highest score in one coordinate dominates everything also does not give an α-fraction of voters for large n.

**Solution 2** gives k/(k+1). Its argument is not sound. It claims the best committee member beats an outsider a for a fraction k/(k+1) of voters. But that fraction is the chance that at least one member beats a, not the fraction of voters preferring a single fixed member. Its first-moment argument is also asserted rather than derived.

**Solution 3** uses an i.i.d. uniform score representation, which is the right framework. The outsider a escapes domination if it beats all k committee members in at least t ≈ n(1−α) voters. The probability of this near the extreme scales as a power of the extreme-score scale, which leads to an expected number of dominating committees of order m^{k−n/t}. This is a genuine scaling argument.

I did a rough check of the k=1 case. A single candidate b with all scores near 1 has an outsider-beating region of volume about ε^t. With ε ≈ m^{-1/n}, that gives m^{1−t/n} → ∞ outsiders unless t is of order n. This is consistent with a threshold of 0 at k=1, matching 1 − 1/k, though the check is heuristic because unbalanced choices of b were not ruled out.

The condition k > n/t ≈ 1/(1−α) gives the threshold α* = 1 − 1/k.

CHOICE: 3
